text: 3 Preliminaries
3.1 Notation and Problem Definition

A graph can be represented as [MATH G=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})] , where [MATH \mathcal{V}=\{v_{1},...,v_{n}\}] is the node set and [MATH \mathcal{E}] is the edge set. In many applications where nodes have attributes, we augment [MATH G] with the node feature set [MATH \mathcal{X}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},...,\mathbf{x}_{n}\}] where [MATH \mathbf{x}_{i}] is the feature vector associated with node [MATH v_{i}] .

Predictions on graphs are made by first embedding nodes into a low-dimensional space which is then fed into a classifier, potentially in an end-to-end fashion. Specifically, a node embedding model can be written as a function [MATH f:\mathcal{V}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}] that maps nodes [MATH \mathcal{V}] to [MATH d] -dimensional vectors [MATH \mathcal{Z}=\{\mathbf{z}_{1},...,\mathbf{z}_{n}\},\mathbf{z}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}] .
3.2 Limitations of Structure-aware Embeddings

Our goal is to learn embeddings that capture the local network structure as well as retain the global network position of a given node. We call node embeddings to be position-aware, if the embedding of two nodes can be used to (approximately) recover their shortest path distance in the network. This property is crucial for many prediction tasks, such as link prediction and community detection. We show below that GNN-based embeddings cannot recover shortest path distances between nodes, which may lead to suboptimal performance in tasks where such information is needed.

A node embedding [MATH \mathbf{z}_{i}=f_{p}(v_{i}),\forall v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}] is position-aware if there exists a function [MATH g_{p}(\cdot,\cdot)] such that [MATH d_{sp}(v_{i},v_{j})=g_{p}(\mathbf{z}_{i},\mathbf{z}_{j})] , where [MATH d_{sp}(\cdot,\cdot)] is the shortest path distance in [MATH G] .

A node embedding [MATH \mathbf{z}_{i}=f_{s_{q}}(v_{i}),\forall v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}] is structure-aware if it is a function of up to [MATH q] -hop network neighbourhood of node [MATH v_{i}] . Specifically, [MATH \mathbf{z}_{i}=g_{s}(N_{1}(v_{i}),...,N_{q}(v_{i}))] , where [MATH N_{k}(v_{i})] is the set of the nodes [MATH k] -hops away from node [MATH v_{i}] , and [MATH g_{s}] can be any function.

For example, most graph neural networks compute node embeddings by aggregating information from each node’s [MATH q] -hop neighborhood, and are thus structure-aware. In contrast, (long) random-walk-based embeddings such as DeepWalk and Node2Vec are position-aware, since their objective function forces nodes that are close in the shortest path to also be close in the embedding space. In general, structure-aware embeddings cannot be mapped to position-aware embeddings. Therefore, when the learning task requires node positional information, only using structure-aware embeddings as input is not sufficient:

There exists a mapping [MATH g] that maps structure-aware embeddings [MATH f_{s_{q}}(v_{i}),\forall v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}] to position-aware embeddings [MATH f_{p}(v_{i}),\forall v_{i}\in\mathcal{V}] , if and only if no pair of nodes have isomorphic local [MATH q] -hop neighbourhood graphs.

Proposition 1 is proved in the Appendix. The proof is based on the identifiability arguments similar to the proof of Theorem 1 in (Hamilton et al., 2017a), and also explains why in some cases GNNs may perform well in tasks requiring positional information. However, in real-world graphs such as molecules and social networks, the structural equivalences between nodes’ local neighbourhood graphs are quite common, making GNNs hard to identify different nodes. Furthermore, the mapping [MATH g] essentially memorizes the shortest path distance between a pair of structure-aware node embeddings whose local neighbourhoods are unique. Therefore, even if the GNN perfectly learns the mapping [MATH g] , it cannot generalize to the mapping to new graphs.
4 Proposed Approach

In this section, we first describe the P-GNN framework that extends GNNs to learn position-aware node embeddings. We follow by a discussion on our model designing choices. Last, we theoretically show how P-GNNs generalize existing GNNs and learn position-aware embeddings.
4.1 The Framework of P-GNNs

We propose Position-aware Graph Neural Networks that generalize the concepts of Graph Neural Networks with two key insights. First, when computing the node embedding, instead of only aggregating messages computed from a node’s local network neighbourhood, we allow P-GNNs to aggregate messages from anchor-sets, which are randomly chosen subsets of all the nodes (Figure 2, left). Note that anchor sets get resampled every time the model is run forward. Secondly, when performing message aggregation, instead of letting each node aggregate information independently, the aggregation is coupled across all the nodes in order to distinguish nodes with different positions in the network (Figure 2, middle). We design P-GNNs such that each node embedding dimension corresponds to messages computed with respect to one anchor-set, which makes the computed node embeddings position-aware (Figure 2, right).

P-GNNs contain the following key components: [MATH \bullet] [MATH k] anchor-sets [MATH S_{i}] of different sizes. [MATH \bullet] Message computation function [MATH F] that combines feature information of two nodes with their network distance. [MATH \bullet] Matrix [MATH \mathbf{M}] of anchor-set messages, where each row [MATH i] is an anchor-set message [MATH \mathcal{M}_{i}] computed by [MATH F] . [MATH \bullet] Trainable aggregation functions [MATH \textsc{Agg}_{M}] , [MATH \textsc{Agg}_{S}] that aggregate/transform feature information of the nodes in the anchor-set and then also aggregate it across the anchor-sets. [MATH \bullet] Trainable vector [MATH \mathbf{w}] that projects message matrix [MATH \mathbf{M}] to a lower-dimensional embedding space [MATH \mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}] .

Algorithm 1 summarizes the general framework of P-GNNs. A P-GNN consists of multiple P-GNN layers. Concretely, the [MATH l^{\text{th}}] P-GNN layer first samples [MATH k] random anchor-sets [MATH S_{i}] . Then, the [MATH i^{\text{th}}] dimension of the output node embedding [MATH \mathbf{z}_{v}] represents messages computed with respect to the [MATH i^{\text{th}}] anchor-set [MATH S_{i}] . Each dimension of the embedding is obtained by first computing the message from each node in the anchor-set via message computation function [MATH F] , then applying a message aggregation function [MATH \textsc{Agg}_{M}] , and finally applying a non-linear transformation to get a scalar via weights [MATH \mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}] and non-linearity [MATH \sigma] . Specifically, the message from each node includes distances that reveal node positions as well as feature-based information from input node features. The message aggregation functions are the same class of functions as used by existing GNNs. We further elaborate on the design choices in Section 4.3.

P-GNNs are position-aware. The output embeddings [MATH \mathbf{z}_{v}] are position-aware, as each dimension of the embedding encodes the necessary information to distinguish structurally equivalent nodes that reside in different parts of the graph. Note that if we permute the dimensions of all the node embeddings [MATH \mathbf{z}_{v}] , the resulting embeddings are equivalent to the original embeddings because they carry the same node positional information with respect to (permuted order of) anchor-sets [MATH \{S_{i}\}] .

Multiple P-GNN layers can be naturally stacked to achieve higher expressive power. Note that unlike GNNs, we cannot feed the output embeddings [MATH \mathbf{z}_{v}] from the previous layer to the next layer, because the dimensions of [MATH \mathbf{z}_{v}] can be arbitrarily permuted; therefore, applying a fixed non-linear transformation over this representation is problematic. The deeper reason we cannot feed [MATH \mathbf{z}_{v}] to the next layer is that the position of a node is always relative to the chosen anchor-sets; thus, canonical position-aware embeddings do not exist. Therefore, P-GNNs also compute structure-aware messages [MATH \mathbf{h}_{v}] , which are computed via an order-invariant message aggregation function that aggregates messages across anchor-sets, and are then fed into the next P-GNN layer as input.
4.2 Anchor-set Selection

We rely on Bourgain’s Theorem to guide the choice of anchor-sets, such that the resulting representations are guaranteed to have low distortion. Specifically, distortion measures the faithfulness of the embeddings in preserving distances when mapping from one metric space to another metric space, which is defined as follows:

Given two metric spaces [MATH (\mathcal{V},d)] and [MATH (\mathcal{Z},d^{\prime})] and a function [MATH f:\mathcal{V}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}] , [MATH f] is said to have distortion [MATH \alpha] if [MATH \forall u,v\in\mathcal{V}] , [MATH \frac{1}{\alpha}d(u,v)\leq d^{\prime}(f(u),f(v))\leq d(u,v)] .
Theorem 1 states the Bourgain Theorem (Bourgain, 1985), which shows the existence of a low distortion embedding that maps from any metric space to the [MATH l_{p}] metric space:

(Bourgain theorem) Given any finite metric space [MATH (\mathcal{V},d)] with [MATH |\mathcal{V}|=n] , there exists an embedding of [MATH (\mathcal{V},d)] into [MATH \mathbb{R}^{k}] under any [MATH l_{p}] metric, where [MATH k=O(\log^{2}n)] , and the distortion of the embedding is [MATH O(\log n)] .
A constructive proof of Theorem 1 (Linial et al., 1995) provides an algorithm to construct an [MATH O(\log^{2}n)] dimensional embedding via anchor-sets, as summarized in Theorem 2:

(Constructive proof of Bourgain theorem) For metric space [MATH (\mathcal{V},d)] , given [MATH k=c\log^{2}n] random sets [MATH S_{i,j}\subset\mathcal{V},i=1,2,...,\log n,j=1,2,...,c\log n] where [MATH c] is a constant, [MATH S_{i,j}] is chosen by including each point in [MATH \mathcal{V}] independently with probability [MATH \frac{1}{2^{i}}] . An embedding method for [MATH v\in\mathcal{V}] is defined as:
[MATH f(v)=\big(\frac{d(v,S_{1,1})}{k},\frac{d(v,S_{1,2})}{k},...,\frac{d(v,S_{\log n,c\log n})}{k}\big)] (1)
where [MATH d(v,S_{i,j})=\min_{u\in S_{i,j}}d(v,u)] . Then, [MATH f] is an embedding method that satisfies Theorem 1.

The proposed P-GNNs can be viewed as a generalization of the embedding method in Theorem 2, where the distance metric [MATH d] is generalized via message computation function [MATH F] and message aggregation function [MATH \textsc{Agg}_{M}] that accounts for both node feature information and position-based similarities (Section 4.3). Using this analogy, Theorem 2 offers two insights for selecting anchor-sets in P-GNNs. First, [MATH O(\log^{2}n)] anchor-sets are needed to guarantee low distortion embedding. Second, these anchor-sets have sizes distributed exponentially. Here, we illustrate the intuition behind selecting anchor-sets with different sizes via the [MATH 1] -hop shortest path distance defined in Equation 2. Suppose that the model is computing embeddings for node [MATH v_{i}] . We say an anchor-set hits node [MATH v_{i}] if [MATH v_{i}] or any of its one-hop neighbours is included in the anchor-set. Small anchor-sets can provide positional information with high certainty, because when a small anchor-set hits [MATH v_{i}] , we know that [MATH v_{i}] is located close to one of the very few nodes in the small anchor-set. However, the probability that such small anchor-set hits [MATH v_{i}] is low, and the anchor-set is uninformative if it misses [MATH v_{i}] . On the contrary, large anchor-sets have higher probability of hitting [MATH v_{i}] , thus sampling large anchor-sets can result in high sample efficiency. However, knowing that a large anchor-set hits [MATH v_{i}] provides little information about its position, since [MATH v_{i}] might be close to any of the many nodes in the anchor-set. Therefore, choosing anchor-sets of different sizes balances the trade-off and leads to efficient embeddings.

Following the above principle, P-GNNs choose [MATH k=c\log^{2}n] random anchor-sets, denoted as [MATH S_{i,j}\subset\mathcal{V}] , where [MATH i=1,\dots,\log n,j=1,\dots,c\log n] and [MATH c] is a hyperparameter. To sample an anchor-set [MATH S_{i,j}] , we sample each node in [MATH \mathcal{V}] independently with probability [MATH \frac{1}{2^{i}}] .
4.3 Design decisions for P-GNNs
In this section, we discuss the design choices of the two key components of P-GNNs: the message computation function [MATH F] and the message aggregation functions Agg.

Message Computation Function [MATH F] . Message computation function [MATH F(v,u,\mathbf{h}_{v},\mathbf{h}_{u})] has to account for both position-based similarities as well as feature information. Position-based similarities are the key to reveal a node’s positional information, while feature information may include other side information that is useful for the prediction task.

Position-based similarities can be computed via the shortest path distance, or, for example, personalized PageRank (Jeh & Widom, 2003). However, since the computation of shortest path distances has a [MATH O(|\mathcal{V}|^{3})] computational complexity, we propose the following [MATH q] -hop shortest path distance
[MATH d^{q}_{sp}(v,u)=\begin{cases}d_{sp}(v,u),&\text{if }d_{sp}(v,u)\leq q,\\ \infty,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}] (2)

where [MATH d_{sp}] is the shortest path distance between a pair of nodes. Note that [MATH 1] -hop distance can be directly identified from the adjacency matrix, and thus no additional computation is needed. Since we aim to map nodes that are close in the network to similar embeddings, we further transform the distance [MATH s(v,u)=\frac{1}{d^{q}_{sp}(v,u)+1}] to map it to a [MATH (0,1)] range.

Feature information can be incorporated into [MATH \mathbf{h}_{u}] by passing in the information from the neighbouring nodes, as in GCN (Kipf & Welling, 2017), or by concatenating node features [MATH \mathbf{h}_{v}] and [MATH \mathbf{h}_{u}] , similar to GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017a), although other approaches like attention can be used as well (Velickovic et al., 2018). Combining position and feature information can then be achieved via concatenation or product. We find that simple product works well empirically. Specifically, we find the following message passing function [MATH F] performs well empirically
[MATH F(v,u,\mathbf{h}_{v},\mathbf{h}_{u})=s(v,u)\textsc{concat}(\mathbf{h}_{v},\mathbf{h}_{u})] (3)

Message Aggregation Functions Agg. Message aggregation functions aggregate information from a set of messages (vectors). Any permutation invariant function, such as [MATH \textsc{Mean},\textsc{Min},\textsc{Max},\textsc{Sum}] , can be used, and non-linear transformations are often applied before and/or after the aggregation to achieve higher expressive power (Zaheer et al., 2017). We find that using simple Mean aggregation function provides good results, thus we use it to instantiate both [MATH \textsc{Agg}_{M}] and [MATH \textsc{Agg}_{S}] .
5.3 Complexity Analysis

In P-GNNs, every node communicates with [MATH O(\log^{2}n)] anchor-sets in a graph with [MATH n] nodes and [MATH e] edges. Suppose on average each anchor-set contains [MATH m] nodes, then there are [MATH O(mn\log^{2}n)] message communications in total. In contrast, the number of communications is [MATH O(ne)] for existing GNNs. The complexity of P-GNN does not depend on the average degree of nodes in [MATH G] , and thus P-GNN will be more efficient than a GNN of the graph is dense. In practice, we also observe that the computation can be sped up by using a simplified aggregation [MATH \textsc{Agg}_{S}] , while only slightly sacrificing predictive performance. Here for each anchor-set, we only aggregate message from the node closest to a given node [MATH v] . This will remove the factor [MATH m] in the complexity of P-GNNs, making the complexity [MATH O(n\log^{2}n)] . We use this implementation in the experiments.
